title: Arrays and hashing
recognize: You need counts, fast lookup, or to preserve the order of a collection.
approach: State the input and edge cases, choose a map or set when repeated lookup dominates, then trace a small example.
hint: Ask what information must be remembered after seeing each item.

title: String transformation
recognize: The answer depends on characters, word boundaries, or symmetry.
approach: Define how to normalize the input, then decide whether one pass or two pointers is enough.
hint: Write down how empty input, punctuation, and ties should behave.

title: Iteration and recursion
recognize: A task repeats a small rule over a range or nested structure.
approach: Choose a loop or recursive state, identify the base case, and test the smallest input first.
hint: Make the stopping condition explicit before handling the general case.

title: Two pointers and windows
recognize: You need a contiguous range or a pair of positions moving through ordered data.
approach: Track the meaning of both boundaries and update an invariant after every move.
hint: Ask what fact lets one boundary move without losing a valid answer.

title: Dynamic programming
recognize: Overlapping smaller subproblems determine the answer for a larger prefix.
approach: Define one state in a sentence, write the transition, and verify base rows or columns.
hint: Let the state represent the best answer for two prefixes.

title: Stacks and monotonic structure
recognize: The most recent unmatched item or a boundary of increasing heights matters.
approach: State what the stack stores and when an item must be removed.
hint: A stack can remember the boundary before a valid region starts.

title: Binary search on partitions
recognize: A sorted input lets you discard half the search space after one comparison.
approach: Define a valid partition, test its boundary cases, then move toward the violated side.
hint: Search the smaller array's partition instead of merging both arrays.

title: Graphs and heaps
recognize: The next best candidate or a shortest sequence of transitions matters.
approach: Model states and transitions, choose BFS for equal-cost steps or a heap for ordered frontiers.
hint: Ask whether each step has equal cost and what must be visited only once.
